findings.claim: The model answer credits the 2018 labelling rule with formalising the Yamanashi and Hokkaido GIs, and the stem calls it a 'law of 2018'.
findings.because: The NTA labelling standard was issued on 30 October 2015 and took effect on 30 October 2018. The GIs have nothing to do with it: Yamanashi was designated on 16 July 2013, under the separate GI notification, and Hokkaido on 27 June 2018. The standard's own provisions are the 'Japan Wine' term (grapes grown in Japan and wine made in Japan) and the 85% rule for naming a region on the label.

Those standards created "Japan Wine" (grapes harvested in Japan, wine produced and bottled in Japan) in place of the old "Domestic Wine" term. findings.claim: The stem and model answer treat 'Deutscher Crémant' as a German label category and say it requires whole-bunch pressing.
findings.because: Under EU Delegated Regulation 2019/33, 'Crémant' may only be used on a quality sparkling wine with a PDO. The term must appear together with the name of the geographical unit behind that PDO, so in Germany the wine is a Sekt b.A. labelled as, for example, 'Crémant' with 'Pfalz' or 'Baden'. There is no national 'Deutscher Crémant' designation. The same regulation allows pressing of whole or destemmed grapes (at most 100 litres per 150 kg), so whole-bunch pressing is not a legal requirement.
findings.fix: Stem: '...Sekt, Deutscher Sekt, Sekt b.A., Winzersekt and Crémant each guarantee?' Answer sentence: "'Crémant' (always paired with the region's name, e.g. Crémant from the Pfalz, and therefore always a Sekt b.A.) follows the EU Crémant rules: hand-harvesting, pressing of whole or destemmed grapes at no more than 100 litres per 150 kg, traditional method, at least nine months on lees."
findings.verifyReason: The finding holds on both counts. (1) German law has no "Deutscher Crémant" category. WeinV 1995 § 34a allows the word "Crémant" only on a Sekt b.A. that meets Art. 53(5) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/33, and the label must also carry the protected origin name. Art. 53(5) says "Crémant" appears alongside the name of the geographical unit. So the wine is a regional Crémant (for example from the Pfalz), not a national "Deutscher" one. (2) Art. 53(5)(b) requires must "obtained by pressing whole or destemmed grapes", with no more than 100 litres per 150 kg. Whole-bunch pressing is therefore permitted but not required, so the model answer's "whole-bunch pressing" is a false statement of the legal rule. The examiner's fix is accurate: manual harvest (53(5)(a)), whole or destemmed grapes at 100 L/150 kg, traditional method with at least nine months on lees (through 53(4)), always a Sekt b.A. with the region named. The accept list does not mention Crémant and needs no change. The VDP sentence describes a private statute and is outside this finding.
findings.finalFix: Stem: "Read a German sparkling label: what do Sekt, Deutscher Sekt, Sekt b.A., Winzersekt and Crémant each guarantee?" Replace the answer's Crémant sentence with: "'Crémant' (always paired with the region's name, e.g. Crémant from the Pfalz, and therefore always a Sekt b.A.) follows the EU Crémant rules: hand-harvesting, pressing of whole or destemmed grapes at no more than 100 litres per 150 kg, traditional method, at least nine months on lees."

question.q: Read a German sparkling label: what do Sekt, Deutscher Sekt, Sekt b.A., Winzersekt and Deutscher Cremant each guarantee?
accept: sekt may use imported base wine deutscher sekt is all german sekt ba comes from one named region winzersekt is estate fruit by the traditional method
winzersekt means the grower's own fruit bottle fermented with at least nine months on the lees
deutscher sekt guarantees german grapes and sekt ba guarantees one of the thirteen regions
question.ans: 'Sekt' on its own guarantees almost nothing about origin: the base wine may be bought anywhere in the EU and for the big industrial brands it is, typically Italian, Spanish or French; expect tank method, minimal ageing and a wine sold on brand rather than place. 'Deutscher Sekt' means the grapes are 100% German. 'Sekt b.A.' — bestimmter Anbaugebiete — means all the fruit comes from a single one of the thirteen designated regions, which must be named on the label. 'Winzersekt' is the grower tier: estate's own fruit, traditional method, bottle-fermented and aged a minimum of nine months on the lees, with vintage and variety declared. 'Deutscher Cremant' follows the EU Cremant rules — whole-bunch pressing at a restricted juice yield, traditional method, at least nine months on lees. Above all of it sits the VDP's own Sekt statute, which requires hand-harvesting, whole-bunch pressing and substantially longer lees ageing than the law asks. The working shortcut for a list: if the label does not say Winzersekt, Cremant, or 'traditionelle Flaschengarung' with a named grower behind it, treat it as industrial.
question.exp: Germany drinks more sparkling wine per head than almost anywhere and the overwhelming majority of it tells you nothing about where it grew — which is exactly why the label hierarchy is worth knowing cold. The grower tier is genuinely serious and still underpriced: Raumland, Griesel, Barth, Solter and Schembs make traditional-method wine at a quality that would cost twice as much with a Champagne address, and Riesling Sekt is a category with no real competitor.
